chunks.text:
Hi Alexis,

I've been thinking a lot about reframe. Less the product itself than the act of building, and the particular shape of difficulty you've chosen.



Here's something I keep returning to: women-founded startups generate 78 cents of revenue per dollar invested. Male-founded companies generate 31 cents. The ratio is 2.5:1 in your favor. Yet women receive 2.3% of venture capital.[^bcg] Much of the disparity comes down to the questions. Investors ask women "what could go wrong?" while asking men "what could go right?"[^pattern] The evaluation is ::structurally tilted:: before you even walk into the room.

You already know this. You live it. I'm telling you that I see it, and that the seeing doesn't diminish what you're doing.

---

Paul Graham writes that after a while determination starts to look like talent.[^pg] "There are plenty of people as smart as Bill Gates who achieve nothing." Intelligence is common. The willingness to keep going when the evidence suggests you shouldn't is rare.

Early-stage startups are fragile. Almost all of them. The question venture asks is how big this could get if the founders do the right things. Lending asks for evidence. Venture asks for conviction: "I'll see it when I believe it."

You're in the phase Graham describes as keeping a fire contained at first to get it really hot before adding more logs.[^scale] Doing things that don't scale is how you learn what actually matters.

---

Hannah Arendt writes that the miracle that saves the world from its "natural" ruin is the fact of natality: that humans are born, and can begin something genuinely new.[^arendt] Starting a company is a form of that. The world wasn't asking for reframe. The world doesn't ask for anything. It just continues.

---

Reid Hoffman describes founding as jumping off a cliff and assembling an airplane on the way down.[^hoffman] There's no stable ground. The building happens during the falling.

Every founder in one study used "lonely" to describe the experience. 5.5:1 ratio compared to general population for experiencing isolation.  You're holding a vision no one else can fully see, asking others to trust what you see.



I don't have a remedy for the loneliness. I don't think there is one. I can only say: I see you carrying it. I believe in what you're building, before the evidence, because belief before evidence is what this phase requires.

---

I choose to believe in you. In your ability to do the painful schleps that other people's minds won't even let them see.[^schlep] In your capacity to hold the fire contained until it's hot enough.

The pattern-matching says you'll be asked the wrong questions. None of that changes what you're capable of.

Build reframe. I'll be here, will support you along the way, watching it become real.

[^sign]

[^bcg]: boston consulting group and masschallenge, "why women-owned startups are a better bet" (2018): 78 vs 31 cents of _revenue_ per dollar of funding, not investor returns. the 2.3% is pitchbook's figure for all-female founding teams in 2020.

[^pattern]: dana kanze et al., "we ask men to win and women not to lose," _academy of management journal_ (2018): VCs asked male founders promotion questions and female founders prevention questions, and the question type predicted funding. it sits on the "lack of fit" model from organizational psychology: women expected to be less capable in male-typed domains unless objective evidence proves otherwise. early-stage VC operates under high uncertainty without track records.

[^pg]: paul graham, "the anatomy of determination" (2009). "after a while determination starts to look like talent." also: "there are plenty of people as smart as bill gates who achieve nothing."

[^scale]: paul graham, "do things that don't scale" (2013). "it's like keeping a fire contained at first to get it really hot before adding more logs." the most successful startups had to work hard to delight their first users.

[^arendt]: hannah arendt, _the human condition_ (1958). natality as the ontological root of action. the capacity to begin something new, to interrupt the expected order.

[^hoffman]: reid hoffman, a line he has repeated in talks and interviews for years, in several wordings. 

[^schlep]: paul graham, "schlep blindness" (2012). your unconscious won't even let you see ideas that involve painful schleps. most people's minds refuse to consider certain hard problems.
